title: The Birthday Money
prompt: You got $40 in birthday cards. Your mom says you can keep $10 in your wallet and put the rest "somewhere it can grow." You're not sure what that means.
method_guidance: This is money you now own, and a choice about where to keep it: your wallet, or a bank.
It came from people who love you giving you a gift, not from work — but it's still yours to manage.
You're not agreeing to anything yet, but choosing to save some means agreeing to wait to spend it.
Money in a savings account is safe and can slowly earn a little more money over time; money in your wallet can't grow, and it can get lost.
Ask a grown-up to show you the account balance online or on a receipt, so the number matches what you put in.

title: The Countdown Skin
prompt: A game you love shows a glowing outfit for your character. A red clock is counting down: "Only 2 hours left! Buy now for 500 gems." You have 300 gems saved up.
method_guidance: This is a virtual item — a costume for your character that only exists inside this one game.
The gems either came from time you already spent playing, or from real money a grown-up paid to buy them.
You're agreeing to trade something you have (gems, or a grown-up's money) for something you can only use in this game.
The outfit might get boring in a week, or the game could change and take it away — but the gems or money spent are gone either way.
Ask: would I still want this if the clock wasn't counting down? Countdown clocks are designed to make you decide fast, not carefully.

title: Grandma's Gift Card
prompt: Grandma gives you a $25 gift card to a toy store's app. It shows a balance on the screen, but it doesn't look like real cash.
method_guidance: This is a gift card — a stored amount of spending power that only works at one store or app.
The value came from Grandma paying real money to load the card for you.
You're agreeing to spend it only where the card works, and once it's spent, it can't turn back into cash.
If you don't use it, the balance usually just sits there — some cards even lose value over time, so it's smart to use it before too long.
Check the real balance in the app or on the receipt after you buy something, so you always know what's left.

title: The Free Coins Video
prompt: A video pops up: a cartoon character says "Type your username here and get 10,000 free game coins right now!" It looks fun and colorful.
method_guidance: This is an ad or website pretending it can give you free game currency just for typing your info.
Real game coins only come from the actual game company — not from a random outside site or video.
By typing your username or password there, you'd be agreeing to hand over your account to strangers.
"Free coins" sites almost never work — instead, they can steal your account, your saved items, or trick a grown-up's card into being charged.
The only place to trust for coins is the real game app or website. When in doubt, ask a grown-up before typing anything.

title: Mom's Phone Wallet
prompt: At the store, Mom taps her phone on a little machine instead of using cash, and the cashier says "Thank you!" No money or card ever came out.
method_guidance: This is a digital wallet — Mom's phone is standing in for a debit or credit card that's connected to her bank account.
The money is coming straight out of Mom's real bank account, the same as if she'd swiped a card.
By tapping, she's agreeing to pay the store the exact amount shown on the screen.
Her bank balance goes down right away (or very soon), just like paying with cash — the phone just made it faster.
A receipt or the banking app will show the exact charge, so she can check it matches what she bought.

title: The Lemonade Stand
prompt: You sell lemonade all afternoon and end up with a jar of $17 in coins and bills. Your dad asks, "What's the plan for this?"
method_guidance: This is money you earned yourself by selling something people wanted — not a gift, not an allowance.
It came from the neighbors who paid you for cups of lemonade.
There's no agreement yet — this is the moment you get to decide: spend some, save some, maybe share some.
Coins in a jar don't grow and can be lost or spent without noticing; money moved to a savings account stays safer and can add up.
Count it together with a grown-up and write the number down, so you can check later that it's all still there.

title: The Stranger Who Says They're an Admin
prompt: Someone messages you in a game: "Hi! I'm a game admin. Send me your login so I can give you a special prize." They have a badge icon next to their name.
method_guidance: This is a message from someone claiming to be in charge of the game — but anyone can put a badge-looking icon in their name.
There's no real prize coming from anywhere; the goal is to get your password so they can take your account and anything in it.
If you sent your login, you'd be agreeing to give a stranger full control of your account.
They could lock you out, spend or trade away everything you've earned, and message your friends pretending to be you.
Real game staff never ask for your password in a chat. Always check with a grown-up before sending any login information to anyone.

title: The Chore Chart App
prompt: Your family uses an app where finishing chores adds "stars" to your name, and every 10 stars turns into $1 in your savings app.
method_guidance: This is a digital way of tracking your earnings — stars for chores that convert into real money.
The money is coming from your parents, as a reward for the work you did around the house.
By doing the chore and tapping it done, you and your parents are agreeing on what work equals what reward.
The stars add up over time into real dollars you can see in the app — but only if the chores actually get marked complete.
Check the app together with a grown-up each week to make sure your stars and your chores actually match up.

title: Big Brother's IOU
prompt: Your older brother is short on cash and asks to borrow $5 from your piggy bank. He promises, "I'll give you back $6 next week."
method_guidance: This is a loan — you're giving up money now with a promise you'll get more back later.
The extra dollar he's promising has to come from his own future money, like his allowance.
By lending it, you're agreeing to wait and trust that he'll actually pay you back the full $6.
He might pay you back exactly as promised — or he might forget, spend his allowance on something else, and you're left waiting.
Write down the deal (how much, and when) so you both remember, and check in on the date you agreed on.

title: The Shiny Coin App
prompt: An ad shows a shiny gold coin: "Collect ShinyCoins in this app — they could be worth real money someday!" Your friend says his cousin made $50 from it.
method_guidance: This is a made-up digital coin inside an app — different from the money in a bank, and different from real coins.
Its value doesn't come from a bank or the government — it only has value if someone else agrees to pay real money for it, which might never happen.
Collecting the coins doesn't cost you anything by itself, but the app is hoping you'll agree to spend real money to get more, faster.
The coins could stay worth nothing forever, or the app could shut down and they'd disappear completely — "could be worth money someday" is not a promise.
Ask a grown-up to help you find out if anyone has actually turned these coins into real money, or if it's just an ad's story.
